questions.junior_answer: Control for other variables like age and spend in a regression.
questions.senior_answer: First I'd learn how discounts were assigned: if marketing targeted engaged customers, or at-risk customers, the groups differ before treatment. I'd map the likely causal structure, then compare like with like: propensity-score matching or weighting, or regression adjustment on pre-treatment covariates only. If there is a rollout date, a region or an eligibility cutoff, difference-in-differences or regression discontinuity gives a stronger estimate. I'd check covariate balance and run a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured factors. Adjustment only handles what we measured, so I'd say so and recommend a small holdout experiment going forward.

questions.question: Your A/B test has 100,000 users per arm and a 2% click rate. How do you compute a confidence interval for the difference in click rates?

follow_ups.text: What are the assumptions behind that formula?
follow_ups.intent: test independence and the normal approximation

variants.text: Some users appear in both arms because they used two devices. Does your interval still hold?
When does the normal approximation for a difference in proportions break down?

follow_ups.text: What if randomization was by user but you count clicks per session?

variants.text: You randomized by user, but your analysis treats each page view as independent. What happens to your interval?
Heavy users generate 20% of sessions. Why does that matter when the unit of analysis is the session?

follow_ups.text: How would you check the result without a formula?

variants.text: How would you use the bootstrap to get the same interval? What do you resample?
How could you simulate the experiment to check that your formula gives intervals of the right width?

questions.key_insight: The unit you randomize on must be the unit you analyze. Otherwise the standard error is too small.
questions.junior_answer: Compare 2% to the other arm's rate and see which is larger.
questions.senior_answer: With p1 and p2 as the arm rates, the standard error of the difference is sqrt(p1(1-p1)/n1 + p2(1-p2)/n2), and the 95% interval is the difference plus or minus 1.96 times that. For about 2% and 100,000 users per arm the standard error is roughly 0.063 percentage points, so differences under about 0.12 points are inside the noise. The formula assumes independent users and a large enough n for the normal approximation, both fine here. A common error is analyzing clicks or sessions while randomizing users, which understates variance; I'd analyze per user or use cluster-robust errors. A bootstrap is a good cross-check.

questions.question: Users in your experiment interact with each other, as in a marketplace or a social feature. Does a standard A/B test still work?
questions.context: Senior DS interview at a marketplace or social company

follow_ups.text: What would the bias look like in a two-sided marketplace?

variants.text: In a ride-sharing test, treated riders get faster matches by taking drivers from control riders. Which way does that bias the estimate?
In a social feature, treated users share more, and their control-group friends see more content. Is the effect overstated or understated?

follow_ups.text: What design alternatives exist?
follow_ups.intent: test cluster, switchback and geo experiments

variants.text: You can't randomize individual sellers without them interacting. What experimental designs could you use instead?
When would a switchback design work better than a geo experiment?

follow_ups.text: How would you know the effect is leaking between groups?

variants.text: How could you test whether spillover between groups is present in your experiment?
The control group's metrics moved during the test even though nothing changed for them. What does that suggest?

questions.key_insight: A standard test assumes one user's outcome does not depend on others' assignments. When users interact, control is contaminated and the measured lift is biased.
questions.junior_answer: Yes, just randomize users into two groups.
questions.senior_answer: It can mislead. A/B tests assume one user's outcome doesn't depend on anyone else's assignment. In a marketplace, treated buyers who grab limited inventory take it from control buyers, so the measured lift overstates what launching to everyone would deliver. In social products, treated users influence their control friends, which shrinks the measured effect. Better designs randomize at the level where the interaction happens: clusters of connected users, geographies or time-based switchbacks, accepting lower power. I'd compare cluster-level and user-level estimates as a diagnostic and consider modelling the equilibrium effect.

questions.question: Design a system that forecasts weekly cash collections for 20 business units.

follow_ups.text: Would you build one model or twenty? How do you decide?
follow_ups.intent: test global versus per-unit models and hierarchy

variants.text: Five units have three years of history and the rest have under a year. One model or several?
What would a global model with a unit feature give you that twenty separate models wouldn't?

follow_ups.text: How do you keep unit forecasts consistent with the company total?

variants.text: The CFO looks only at the company total, while unit heads look at their own numbers. How do you keep both views consistent?
Unit forecasts add up to 8% more than the company forecast. Which do you adjust?

follow_ups.text: How would the finance team use and challenge the forecast?

variants.text: A unit head says the forecast is too low because a big contract is about to close. How does the system take in that knowledge?
What would you show finance so they can see why the forecast moved this week?

questions.key_insight: The model is the smaller part. Hierarchy, backtesting, data freshness and how finance will challenge the numbers drive the design.
questions.junior_answer: Train a time-series model for each business unit and run it weekly.
questions.senior_answer: I'd start with the decision: the horizon, the accuracy needed and who acts on it. Data: invoices, payment terms, collection history and calendar effects, from a pipeline with freshness and quality checks. Modelling: a global gradient-boosted model with unit features usually beats twenty small series, with a simple per-unit baseline to compare against; hierarchical reconciliation keeps unit forecasts summing to the total. Evaluation: rolling-origin backtests by horizon, tracking error by unit. Serving: a weekly batch with forecast intervals, versioned outputs, and a view where finance can see drivers and adjust assumptions. Monitoring compares forecasts to actuals as they land and alerts on drift.

questions.question: Design a daily pipeline that ingests transactions from five source systems with inconsistent schemas.

follow_ups.text: How do you detect and handle a schema change at one source?
follow_ups.intent: test schema validation and data contracts

variants.text: One source renamed a column overnight and your pipeline loaded NULLs for a whole day. How should the system have caught it?
How would you agree a data contract with five source teams who all change things on their own schedule?

follow_ups.text: What happens when a run fails halfway?

variants.text: The pipeline loaded three of five sources before failing. What happens when you rerun it?
How do you make the daily load safe to run twice?

follow_ups.text: How do you reconcile the five sources to the same numbers?

variants.text: Total transaction value differs by 2% between your warehouse and the source systems. How do you track down the gap?
Which reconciliation checks would you run every day, and which weekly?

questions.key_insight: Reliability comes from idempotent loads, validation at the boundary and reconciliation, not from the transformation logic.
questions.junior_answer: Write a script per source and combine them into one table.
questions.senior_answer: Land each source's raw data unchanged in a staging area, then transform it into a common canonical schema with explicit mappings and tests. Validate at the boundary: schema, types, null rates, ranges and row counts against expectations, quarantining bad records instead of failing the whole run. Make loads idempotent (partition overwrite or merge on a key) so reruns are safe, orchestrate with retries and alerting, and keep backfills possible. Add reconciliation checks, such as daily totals against each source's control totals, and data contracts with source owners so schema changes are announced. Version the mappings and document lineage.

questions.question: Design an anomaly detection system for key business metrics that analysts will actually trust.

follow_ups.text: How do you handle seasonality and holidays?
follow_ups.intent: test baselines that account for them

variants.text: Sales always drop 40% on public holidays. How do you stop the system alerting every time?
A metric has a strong weekly cycle and a slow upward trend. What baseline would you compare against?

follow_ups.text: How do you keep false alarms down?

variants.text: Analysts received 60 alerts last week and acted on 3. What do you change?
How would you use analysts' responses to alerts to improve the system over time?

follow_ups.text: What would you show alongside an alert?

variants.text: An alert says revenue is down 12% today. What context should come with it so an analyst can act quickly?
How would you point analysts toward which segment or region caused an anomaly?

questions.key_insight: Trust comes from low false alarms and context. An alert that says where the change is and whether it was expected gets used, and a bare red flag gets muted.
questions.junior_answer: Use a z-score and alert when a metric is three standard deviations from the mean.
questions.senior_answer: Start with which metrics matter and the cost of a miss versus a false alarm. Model an expected value that accounts for trend, weekly and yearly seasonality and holidays, such as a forecast with prediction intervals instead of a flat mean, and flag points outside the interval. Reduce noise with minimum-impact thresholds, persistence requirements and grouping of related alerts. With each alert show the metric against its expected range, the segments driving the change (dimension drill-down) and recent related changes such as deployments or data delays, because many anomalies are broken pipelines. Add a feedback button to mark alerts useful or not, track alert precision, and review regularly.

questions.question: Design a semantic search system over 5 million internal documents.
questions.context: Senior DS or ML engineer interview, LLM applications

follow_ups.text: How do you chunk and index the documents?

variants.text: Some documents are 300-page PDFs and others are one-line tickets. How do you chunk them?
What metadata would you store with each chunk, and why?

follow_ups.text: When does pure vector search fail, and what do you add?
follow_ups.intent: test hybrid search with keywords and reranking

variants.text: A user searches for an exact error code and vector search returns loosely related documents. What do you add?
Searches for product names and acronyms perform poorly. Why might embeddings struggle with them?

follow_ups.text: How do you handle permissions?

variants.text: An employee searches and sees a snippet from a document they aren't allowed to open. Where did the design go wrong?
Permissions change daily. How do you keep the search index in sync?

questions.key_insight: Retrieval quality depends on chunking, hybrid ranking and access control more than on the choice of vector database.
questions.junior_answer: Embed the documents and store them in a vector database.
questions.senior_answer: Ingest: parse documents, split them into chunks that preserve meaning with some overlap and metadata (title, source, date, owner), embed each chunk, and store vectors in an approximate nearest-neighbor index alongside the text. Query: embed the query, retrieve candidates, and combine with keyword search (BM25), since exact terms, codes and names are handled poorly by embeddings alone; rerank the top results with a cross-encoder. Enforce permissions at retrieval by filtering on access metadata, not after generation. Keep the index fresh with incremental updates. Evaluate with a labeled set of queries (recall at k, mean reciprocal rank) plus user feedback. Latency and cost scale with index size and reranking depth.

questions.question: Design a what-if scenario tool that lets finance teams see how a forecast changes under different assumptions.

follow_ups.text: How do you make the forecast respond to assumptions the model has never seen?
follow_ups.intent: test combining models with driver-based rules

variants.text: A user asks what happens if prices rise 15%, but prices have never moved more than 3% in your history. How does the tool answer?
Which parts of the scenario should come from the model and which from explicit business rules?

follow_ups.text: How do you show uncertainty?

variants.text: How would you show the range of outcomes for a scenario, not just one line?
Users compare two scenarios whose difference is smaller than the forecast's uncertainty. What do you show them?

follow_ups.text: How do you make sure users don't treat scenarios as predictions?

variants.text: A scenario showing 20% growth ends up in a board deck as the forecast. How could the tool have prevented that?
How would you label scenario outputs so they aren't mistaken for the official forecast?

questions.key_insight: A what-if tool is an explanation tool. Users must see which drivers move the number and understand that scenarios aren't predictions.
questions.junior_answer: Let users change the inputs and rerun the model.
questions.senior_answer: Separate the baseline forecast from a scenario layer: a driver-based structure (volume, price, payment terms, collection rates) that the ML forecast feeds or calibrates, so users change meaningful business levers rather than raw model features, which can produce nonsense outside the training range. Changes are saved as named, versioned scenarios, compared against the baseline, with a waterfall showing each driver's contribution. Show forecast intervals and flag assumptions outside historical ranges. Make recomputation fast with precomputed components or a lightweight surrogate. Label scenarios as 'if' statements, record who changed what, and let finance override with comments.

questions.question: Your LLM feature costs $40,000 a month and the team wants it under $10,000. What do you try, and in what order?
questions.context: Senior DS or ML engineer interview, LLM applications

follow_ups.text: How do you find out where the cost comes from?
follow_ups.intent: test measuring cost per request, per feature and per token type

variants.text: How would you break the $40,000 bill down by feature, prompt and token type?
Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens. How does that change where you look first?

follow_ups.text: How do you check that a cheaper approach hasn't hurt quality?
follow_ups.intent: test evaluation before and after changes

variants.text: You switch most traffic to a smaller model. How do you prove quality didn't drop?
What would you measure before and after adding prompt caching?

follow_ups.text: What would routing between models look like?

variants.text: Describe a setup where a cheap model handles most requests and a stronger one handles the hard ones. How does it decide?
What could go wrong with routing requests between models?

questions.key_insight: Measure before optimizing, then take the cheap wins in order of least quality risk, checking the evaluation set after each change.
questions.junior_answer: Switch to a smaller model.
questions.senior_answer: First I'd instrument cost: tokens in and out per request, per feature, per user type, and find the heavy tail (long prompts, retries, chatty outputs). The lowest-risk savings come first: trim prompts and context, cap output length, cache repeated prefixes and identical requests, and batch non-urgent work. Next, route easy requests to a smaller model and escalate hard ones, or move to a cheaper model for steps that don't need the strongest one. Fine-tuning a small model can pay off at high volume. After every change I'd rerun the evaluation set and track quality, latency and cost together, so a saving that quietly breaks quality is caught. Some of the target may need product changes, such as limiting free usage.

questions.question: What is a generator in Python, and when would you use one instead of a list in a data pipeline?

follow_ups.text: What can you not do with a generator that you can do with a list?
follow_ups.intent: test one-pass iteration and no indexing or length

variants.text: Can you call len() on a generator or slice it like a list? What do you do if you need those?
Why can't you go back to an earlier item in a generator?

follow_ups.text: How would you read and transform a huge file in stages without loading it?

variants.text: Write a pipeline that reads a large log file, filters error lines and parses them, without loading the file.
How would you batch items from a generator into groups of 1,000 for database inserts?

follow_ups.text: What bug appears if you iterate a generator twice?

variants.text: You compute the sum of a generator, then its max, and the max fails. Why?
A function returns a generator, and the caller iterates it twice in a test. What happens?

questions.key_insight: A generator produces values one at a time on demand, so memory stays flat no matter how much data flows through, at the price of single-pass access.
questions.junior_answer: A generator uses yield and saves memory compared to a list.
questions.senior_answer: A generator is a function (or expression) that yields values lazily: it computes the next item only when asked, so memory use does not grow with the data. That suits pipelines that read a large file line by line, transform each record, and write it out, since stages can be chained without ever holding everything. The trade-offs: you can iterate once, you can't index or take len() without consuming it, and iterating twice silently yields nothing the second time, a classic bug. If I need several passes or random access I materialize a list or reload the source. For heavy numeric work I'd still prefer vectorized operations on chunks over item-at-a-time loops.

questions.question: Design a customer churn early-warning system that a retention team uses every week.
questions.context: DS interview, subscription or fintech company

follow_ups.text: How do you define churn so the label is usable?
follow_ups.intent: test label definition and prediction window

variants.text: Customers on annual contracts can only churn at renewal. How do you define the label for them?
Should a customer who downgrades to the free plan count as churned? How do you decide?

follow_ups.text: How do you turn scores into actions the team can take?
follow_ups.intent: test linking predictions to interventions and capacity

variants.text: The team can contact 200 customers a week, but the model flags 1,500 as high risk. How do you prioritize?
Some high-risk customers can't be saved by any offer the team has. How should that affect the list?

follow_ups.text: How do you measure whether the interventions actually helped?

variants.text: Retention went up after launch. How do you know the interventions caused it?
How would you set up a holdout group, and how would you explain the need for it to the retention team?

questions.key_insight: A churn score is only useful if it is tied to an action and a measured result. The prediction is the smallest part of the system.
questions.junior_answer: Train a churn classifier on past customers and send the retention team the top scores.
questions.senior_answer: I'd start with the decision: what can the retention team do, how many customers per week, and how early they need warning. That fixes the churn definition (for example no activity for 60 days) and the prediction window, so labels are usable and not leaked. Features come from usage, billing and support history, built point-in-time in a weekly batch. The model outputs calibrated probabilities, and a layer on top ranks customers by expected value (likelihood times customer value) within the team's capacity, with reasons for each flag. A random holdout group receives no outreach so we can measure real impact, and results feed back into evaluation. Monitoring covers drift, calibration and the outreach results.

questions.question: Design a credit limit decision system whose decisions must be explainable to customers and regulators.
questions.context: Senior DS interview, lending or regulated industry

follow_ups.text: How do you produce reasons for a decision that a customer can understand?
follow_ups.intent: test explanation methods and their limits

variants.text: A customer is declined and asks why. How do you turn SHAP values into a reason they can act on?
Two features with similar effects both appear in the explanation. Which do you show the customer?

follow_ups.text: How do you monitor the system for unfair outcomes?

variants.text: Approval rates differ by 10 points between two age groups. How do you decide whether that's a problem?
Which fairness metrics would you monitor, and why can't you satisfy all of them at once?

follow_ups.text: How do you approve and record a model change?
follow_ups.intent: test governance, versioning and audit trails

variants.text: A regulator asks which model version decided a loan 18 months ago and why. What does your system need to have stored?
Who signs off on a new model version, and what evidence do they need?

questions.key_insight: In a regulated setting the model is only one component. Reasons, fairness checks, change approval and an audit trail are part of the product.
questions.junior_answer: Use a gradient-boosted model and explain it with SHAP.
questions.senior_answer: I'd start with constraints: which inputs are legally allowed, what reasons must be given, and who has to approve changes. Modelling choice is a trade: a constrained or monotonic model (or a scorecard) is easier to defend, while a boosted model with post-hoc explanations may perform better but needs validation that explanations are stable and honest. Each decision stores the inputs, model version, score and top reasons, so any outcome can be reproduced and explained. I'd monitor approval rates and errors across protected groups, plus drift and calibration, and set review gates for model changes with documentation and sign-off from risk and compliance. A human override path handles exceptions.

questions.question: Design a metrics layer so every team computes revenue, active users and churn the same way.

follow_ups.text: Where do metric definitions live, and who can change them?
follow_ups.intent: test ownership and review of definitions

variants.text: Marketing and finance both claim ownership of the 'active user' definition. How do you resolve it?
Where would you store metric definitions so analysts actually use them?

follow_ups.text: How do you handle a definition that needs to change?

variants.text: The business decides 'active user' should now exclude free-trial users. How do you roll that change out?
Historical dashboards will shift when a definition changes. How do you handle that?

follow_ups.text: How do you check that dashboards match the layer?

variants.text: A team's dashboard shows revenue 3% higher than the metrics layer. How would you catch that automatically?
What tests would you run on the metrics layer itself?

questions.key_insight: A metrics layer is a governance problem as much as a technical one. One reviewed definition per metric, versioned, with tests that catch disagreement.
questions.junior_answer: Create a shared table with the metrics so everyone queries the same numbers.
questions.senior_answer: I'd define each metric once, as code in version control, with its grain, filters, time logic and owner, and have dashboards, notebooks and models read through that layer rather than rewriting the SQL. Changes go through review by the owner and the main consumers, and are versioned, with a changelog and a transition period so historical comparisons are not silently broken. Automated tests check the definitions against known totals and compare dashboard outputs to the layer. The layer also handles shared dimensions such as customer segment and time zone. I'd start with the five metrics that cause the most disagreement and expand once teams trust them.

questions.question: What assumptions does linear regression make, and which ones matter most when you only care about prediction?

follow_ups.text: What do you do if the residuals show a pattern?
follow_ups.intent: test diagnosing non-linearity and fixing it with transforms or interactions

variants.text: The residual plot shows a clear U shape. What does that tell you, and what do you change?
Residuals look fine overall but are much larger for one customer segment. What would you try?

follow_ups.text: How do outliers affect it?

variants.text: Three data points with extreme values pull your fitted line noticeably. How do you handle them?
Why does least squares give outliers so much influence compared with absolute error?

follow_ups.text: What changes if you care about inference instead of prediction?
follow_ups.intent: test the difference between predictive and inferential needs

variants.text: Your stakeholder now wants to know how much price affects demand, not just to predict demand. Which assumptions suddenly matter more?
Two features are highly correlated. Does that hurt prediction, inference or both?

questions.key_insight: The assumptions matter in proportion to what you use the model for. Prediction mostly needs a roughly linear, stable relationship, while inference also needs well-behaved errors.
questions.junior_answer: Linearity, independence, normal errors and constant variance.
questions.senior_answer: The classic list is a linear relationship, independent errors, constant error variance, roughly normal errors and no severe collinearity. For pure prediction the ones that bite are linearity (a missed curve means systematic error) and independence across train and test (leakage). Constant variance and normality mostly affect confidence and prediction intervals, not point predictions. Outliers can drag least squares, so I'd check leverage and consider a robust or Huber loss. I'd diagnose with residual plots and fix with transforms, interaction terms or a more flexible model.

questions.question: When would you choose ridge, lasso or elastic net?

follow_ups.text: Why does lasso set some coefficients exactly to zero while ridge does not?
follow_ups.intent: test geometric intuition for L1 versus L2

variants.text: Draw the constraint regions for L1 and L2 penalties. Why does the L1 region produce zeros?
Ridge shrinks a coefficient from 3.0 to 0.1 but never to zero. Why?

follow_ups.text: What happens with a group of highly correlated features?
follow_ups.intent: test lasso instability and elastic net grouping

variants.text: Five features measure nearly the same thing. What does lasso do with them, and what does elastic net do?
Your lasso model picks a different feature from a correlated group each time you resample the data. What would you change?

follow_ups.text: How do you choose the penalty strength?
follow_ups.intent: test cross-validating the penalty and scaling features first

variants.text: How would you pick the lambda for ridge, and why must the features be scaled first?
Cross-validation gives a range of penalties with similar error. Which do you choose, and why?

questions.key_insight: Ridge shrinks every coefficient, lasso also selects features, and elastic net keeps lasso's selection while behaving better with correlated features.
questions.junior_answer: Lasso removes features and ridge shrinks them.
questions.senior_answer: All three add a penalty to reduce variance. Ridge (L2) shrinks coefficients smoothly and keeps every feature, which suits many features that each carry a little signal. Lasso (L1) can set coefficients exactly to zero, so it selects features, which suits sparse problems and interpretability. With correlated features lasso tends to pick one arbitrarily and flip between samples, while elastic net mixes both penalties and tends to keep correlated groups together. I standardize features first, choose the penalty strength by cross-validation, and use time-aware folds for time-ordered data.

questions.question: How does a decision tree choose where to split, and why do deep trees overfit?

follow_ups.text: What is impurity and how is it measured?

variants.text: A node has 80 of one class and 20 of the other. Compute its Gini impurity, and explain what a split is trying to do to it.
Do Gini and entropy usually lead to different trees? Why or why not?

follow_ups.text: How can you stop a tree from overfitting?
follow_ups.intent: test depth limits, minimum leaf size and pruning

variants.text: Your tree has 2,000 leaves, many with a single sample. Which settings would you change?
What is cost-complexity pruning, and how do you choose its strength?

follow_ups.text: Can a tree predict beyond the range of its training data?
follow_ups.intent: test that trees predict piecewise constants

variants.text: Your training data has house sizes up to 300 square meters. What does a tree predict for a 500-square-meter house?
Why are tree-based models a poor choice for extrapolating a trend into the future?

questions.key_insight: A tree greedily picks the split that most reduces impurity, and with no limits it keeps splitting until it memorizes the training data.
questions.junior_answer: It picks the best feature to split on, and deep trees memorize the data.
questions.senior_answer: At each node the tree tries candidate splits on each feature and picks the one that most reduces impurity (Gini or entropy for classification, variance for regression). That is greedy: it does not look ahead. Left unchecked it splits until leaves are nearly pure, so it fits noise and generalizes poorly. Remedies are limiting depth, requiring a minimum number of samples per leaf, pruning, or using an ensemble. A tree predicts piecewise constants, so it cannot extrapolate beyond the training range, which matters for trends.

questions.question: How does a random forest differ from a single tree, and what can go wrong when you read its feature importances?

follow_ups.text: What is out-of-bag error?
follow_ups.intent: test knowing it is a built-in validation estimate

variants.text: How does a random forest estimate its error without a separate validation set?
When can out-of-bag error be misleading?

follow_ups.text: Why are impurity-based importances biased toward some features?
follow_ups.intent: test the bias toward high-cardinality and continuous features

variants.text: A random ID-like feature with many unique values ranks high in impurity importance. Why?
Why do continuous features tend to look more important than binary ones in impurity importance?

follow_ups.text: What would you use instead?

variants.text: How does permutation importance work, and what goes wrong with correlated features?
When would you use SHAP values instead of permutation importance?

questions.key_insight: A forest cuts variance by averaging many decorrelated trees, but its default importances favor features with many possible splits and divide credit between correlated features.
questions.junior_answer: A forest averages many trees, and importance shows which features matter.
questions.senior_answer: Each tree trains on a bootstrap sample and considers a random subset of features at each split, so the trees are decorrelated and averaging them reduces variance without raising bias much. Out-of-bag samples give a built-in validation estimate. Default impurity-based importances are biased toward continuous or high-cardinality features and are computed on training data, so they can reward overfit features; correlated features also split the credit. I'd use permutation importance on held-out data or SHAP, and describe the result as what the model uses, not what causes the outcome.

questions.question: You're choosing between XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost for a tabular problem with many categorical features. How do you decide?

follow_ups.text: How do their tree-growing strategies differ?

variants.text: LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise and XGBoost level-wise by default. What does that mean for overfitting on a small dataset?
Which parameter limits LightGBM's leaf-wise growth, and why does it matter?

follow_ups.text: How does each handle categorical variables?

variants.text: You have a categorical feature with 5,000 levels. How would each of the three libraries handle it?
Why does CatBoost's ordered target statistics approach reduce target leakage?

follow_ups.text: How would you compare them fairly?
follow_ups.intent: test same folds, same tuning budget, and measuring time as well as accuracy

variants.text: One library wins by 0.002 AUC but takes five times longer to train. How do you decide?
How do you make sure each library gets an equal tuning budget?

questions.key_insight: On most tabular data the three land within noise of each other. The choice comes down to categorical handling, speed at your data size and how much tuning you can afford.
questions.junior_answer: XGBoost is the standard, LightGBM is faster and CatBoost handles categories.
questions.senior_answer: All three are gradient-boosted trees, and with equal tuning they are usually within a small margin on accuracy, so I'd decide on practical grounds. LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise with histogram binning, which is fast on large data but can overfit small data without limits on leaves. XGBoost is the most widely deployed and documented, with level-wise growth by default. CatBoost uses ordered target statistics to handle categorical features natively and reduce target leakage, often needing less tuning. With many categoricals I'd start with CatBoost, then compare all three on the same time-aware folds with a fixed tuning budget, looking at accuracy, training time and calibration.

questions.question: Explain how a support vector machine works. When would you use one, and what do you need to do to the data first?

follow_ups.text: What does the kernel trick do?

variants.text: The two classes form concentric circles. How can an SVM separate them?
What does an RBF kernel measure between two points?

follow_ups.text: What do C and gamma control?
follow_ups.intent: test the margin-versus-errors trade-off and kernel width

variants.text: You raise C and training accuracy rises while validation accuracy falls. What's happening?
What happens to the decision boundary as gamma gets very large?

follow_ups.text: Why does an SVM scale poorly to millions of rows?
follow_ups.intent: test training cost growing faster than linearly with rows

variants.text: Training an RBF SVM on 2 million rows hasn't finished after a day. Why, and what alternatives do you have?
When would a linear SVM still be practical at large scale?

questions.key_insight: An SVM finds the boundary with the widest margin, and because margins depend on distances, features must be scaled.
questions.junior_answer: It draws a line between the classes with the biggest gap.
questions.senior_answer: An SVM finds the separating boundary with the largest margin between classes; only the points nearest the boundary, the support vectors, define it. A kernel such as the RBF lets it draw non-linear boundaries by implicitly mapping the data to a higher dimension. C trades margin width against misclassified training points, and gamma sets how local the RBF kernel is. Distances drive everything, so features must be standardized. It works well on small to medium, high-dimensional data like text, but training scales roughly quadratically or worse with rows and its scores are not probabilities, so for large tabular data I'd pick boosting.

questions.question: How does support vector regression differ from ordinary linear regression, and when might you prefer it?

follow_ups.text: What is the epsilon-insensitive loss?
follow_ups.intent: test the idea of a tolerance tube

variants.text: Explain in plain words what the epsilon tube means for errors smaller than epsilon.
How does the choice of epsilon change the model?

follow_ups.text: What happens to points inside the tube?

variants.text: Why does SVR end up depending on only some of the training points?
If you make epsilon larger, what happens to the number of support vectors?

follow_ups.text: How does it compare with ridge for a typical tabular problem?

variants.text: Your dataset has 50 features and 100,000 rows. Would you try SVR or ridge first?
When might SVR's robustness to small errors be a real advantage?

questions.key_insight: SVR ignores errors smaller than a tolerance, so only points outside it shape the model. That makes it robust to small noise, but it is not automatically better than a regularized linear model.
questions.junior_answer: SVR uses support vectors and kernels to fit a curve instead of a line.
questions.senior_answer: Linear regression minimizes squared error on every point. SVR defines a tube of width epsilon around the fit: errors inside the tube cost nothing and errors outside are penalized linearly, with C controlling how heavily. Only points on or outside the tube become support vectors, so the model is sparse and less sensitive to small noise or moderate outliers, and a kernel gives non-linear fits. It needs scaled features and tuning of epsilon, C and gamma. For ordinary tabular regression a regularized linear model or boosting is usually simpler and as good; I'd reach for SVR on smaller, smooth, non-linear problems.

questions.question: How does k-nearest neighbors work, and what are its weaknesses?

questions.key_insight: k-NN has no training step. All of its cost and all of its assumptions sit in the distance function, which breaks down when features are unscaled or numerous.
questions.junior_answer: It looks at the k closest points and takes a vote.
questions.senior_answer: k-NN stores the training data and predicts by taking the majority label (or the average) of the k closest points under a distance metric. Small k gives a jagged, high-variance boundary and large k smooths toward the base rate, so I choose k by cross-validation. Because it uses distance, features must be scaled and irrelevant ones removed; in high dimensions distances become nearly equal, so neighbors stop being meaningful. Prediction is slow on large data without an index or approximate search. It is a useful baseline and underlies many retrieval systems.

questions.question: Naive Bayes assumes features are independent, which is almost never true. Why does it still work, and when would you use it?

follow_ups.text: Where does it fail?

questions.key_insight: Naive Bayes only needs the right class to score highest, not accurate probabilities, so its wrong independence assumption often hurts less than expected.
questions.junior_answer: It's fast and works well for text even though the assumption is wrong.
questions.senior_answer: It multiplies per-feature likelihoods as if features were independent given the class. The assumption is wrong, but classification only needs the correct class to come out on top, and errors from double-counting correlated features often don't change that ordering. Its probabilities are badly calibrated, so I wouldn't use them for cost-based decisions without recalibration. It trains in one pass, needs little data and handles high-dimensional sparse features like words, which is why it is a strong text baseline. Smoothing prevents a single unseen word from zeroing out a class.

questions.question: You fit a logistic regression for loan default. How do you interpret the coefficients, and why might you still choose it over a boosted model?

questions.key_insight: Each coefficient is a change in log-odds with the other features held fixed, and that transparency is often worth a small loss in accuracy.
questions.junior_answer: Positive coefficients increase the chance of default, and it's simple and explainable.
questions.senior_answer: A coefficient is the change in log-odds of default for a one-unit increase in a feature with the others held fixed; exponentiating gives an odds ratio, so 0.7 means about twice the odds. That reading is only safe if features are on comparable scales and not strongly collinear. I'd check linearity in the log-odds and add splines, bins or interactions where needed. I'd keep it over boosting when regulators or stakeholders need clear reasons, when data is small, or when the accuracy gap is within noise, and I'd verify that with a held-out comparison and a calibration check instead of assuming.

questions.key_insight: Unsupervised detectors rank what is unusual, not what is fraudulent, so their value depends on analyst feedback and a threshold tied to review capacity.
questions.junior_answer: Use an isolation forest to flag outliers and review them.
questions.senior_answer: An isolation forest builds random trees that split features at random; points that are isolated in few splits are unusual, so a shorter average path length means a higher anomaly score. I'd engineer behavioral features (amount versus the customer's norm, velocity, new merchant), since raw amounts mostly flag rich customers. With no labels the threshold comes from review capacity: flag the top N per day. Unusual is not the same as fraudulent, so I'd have analysts label a sample from the top of the ranking, measure precision, and feed the labels into a supervised model over time. Segmenting by customer type improves it.

questions.question: You need to model the number of insurance claims per customer per year. Why not just use linear regression, and what would you use?
questions.context: Senior DS interview, insurance or risk

follow_ups.text: What distribution suits count data?

follow_ups.intent: test negative binomial and zero inflation

questions.key_insight: Counts are non-negative integers whose variance grows with the mean, so a model built for counts, with an exposure term, beats a straight line.
questions.junior_answer: Use Poisson regression because it's count data.
questions.senior_answer: Linear regression can predict negative claims and assumes constant variance, but counts are non-negative integers whose variance rises with the mean. A generalized linear model with a log link and a Poisson distribution fits that shape, and coefficients become multiplicative effects on the claim rate. Real claims are often overdispersed (variance above the mean), so I'd check that and move to a negative binomial, or add a zero-inflation component when many customers have none. Customers observed for different periods need an exposure offset so the model predicts a rate. Gradient boosting with a Poisson objective is a flexible alternative.

follow_ups.text: What kinds of cluster shapes does it handle poorly?

questions.key_insight: k-means partitions points by distance to centers, so it assumes roughly round, similar-sized clusters on comparable scales.
questions.junior_answer: It assigns points to the nearest of k centers and then updates the centers.
questions.senior_answer: k-means alternates between assigning each point to its nearest center and moving each center to the mean of its points, until assignments stop changing. It finds a local optimum, so initialization matters; k-means++ and several restarts help. To choose k I'd look at the elbow in within-cluster variance and at silhouette scores, but also at whether the clusters are interpretable and stable across samples. It struggles with elongated or nested shapes, very different cluster sizes and outliers, and it needs scaled numeric features. DBSCAN or Gaussian mixtures are common alternatives.

follow_ups.text: What do eps and min_samples control?

questions.key_insight: DBSCAN groups by density, so it finds odd shapes and flags noise without being told how many clusters exist, but it assumes one density throughout.
questions.junior_answer: DBSCAN doesn't need k and handles outliers.
questions.senior_answer: DBSCAN grows clusters from dense neighborhoods: a point with at least min_samples neighbors within distance eps is a core point, clusters are connected dense regions, and points in no dense region are labeled noise. I'd choose it over k-means when clusters have irregular shapes, when I don't know k, or when outliers are meaningful. It struggles when clusters differ a lot in density, because one eps cannot suit both, and in high dimensions where distances lose meaning. I'd pick eps from a k-distance plot, and features still need scaling.

questions.key_insight: Hierarchical clustering shows how groups merge at every scale, which helps when you don't know how many groups you want or the groups are nested.
questions.junior_answer: It builds a tree of clusters, and you cut it at a level.
questions.senior_answer: Agglomerative clustering starts with each point alone and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters; the dendrogram records every merge and its distance. The linkage rule defines closest: single linkage chains and finds elongated shapes but is noise-sensitive, complete linkage makes compact clusters, and average and Ward sit between. It is useful when the number of groups is unknown or the structure is nested, as with product taxonomies, and I'd pick the cut from large gaps in merge height or from what the business can act on. It needs the pairwise distance matrix, so it is impractical beyond tens of thousands of points without sampling.

questions.question: How are Gaussian mixture models different from k-means, and what do 'soft assignments' give you?

follow_ups.text: How is a mixture model fitted?
follow_ups.intent: test expectation-maximization at a conceptual level

variants.text: Describe in plain words what the E step and the M step do.
Why can a mixture model get stuck in a poor solution, and what do you do about it?

follow_ups.text: What happens if you give the model too many components?
follow_ups.intent: test overfitting and choosing with BIC

variants.text: How would you choose the number of components using BIC?
You fit 20 components to data with 3 real groups. What happens?

follow_ups.text: When would you prefer k-means anyway?

variants.text: The clusters are roughly round and you have 10 million points. Would you use a mixture model?

questions.key_insight: A mixture model gives each point a probability of belonging to each cluster, with clusters of different shapes and sizes, at the cost of more parameters.
questions.junior_answer: A Gaussian mixture gives probabilities instead of hard labels.
questions.senior_answer: k-means is a special case that assumes equal, round clusters and gives hard labels. A Gaussian mixture models the data as a blend of Gaussians, each with its own mean, spread and weight, so clusters can be elliptical and different in size, and each point gets a probability of membership, which is useful for borderline customers or for scoring. It is fitted with expectation-maximization, alternating between computing memberships and updating the Gaussians, and can get stuck in local optima. More components always fit better, so I'd choose the number with BIC or held-out likelihood. k-means is faster and simpler when clusters are roughly round and hard labels are enough.

questions.question: You clustered customers and there are no labels. How do you tell whether the clusters are any good?

follow_ups.text: What do silhouette scores tell you, and what don't they?
follow_ups.intent: test internal metrics and their bias toward round clusters

variants.text: Silhouette is highest at k = 2, but the business wants more detail. How much weight do you put on the silhouette?
Why can silhouette scores favor round, evenly sized clusters?

follow_ups.text: How would you check stability?

variants.text: How would you check whether your clusters change if you resample the customers?

follow_ups.text: What is the business test of a segmentation?
follow_ups.intent: test actionability and difference in behavior

variants.text: Marketing says two of your segments behave the same in campaigns. What does that say about the segmentation?
How would you test whether the segments lead to different results when targeted?

questions.key_insight: Without labels, good means compact and separated, stable under resampling, and different in ways the business can act on. The first two are measurable; the third is the one that matters.
questions.junior_answer: Use the silhouette score and the elbow method.
questions.senior_answer: I'd check three things. Internal quality: silhouette or Davies-Bouldin say whether clusters are compact and separated, but they reward round clusters and can look fine on arbitrary slices. Stability: re-cluster on bootstrap samples or with different seeds and see whether the same groups reappear; unstable clusters are artifacts. Usefulness: profile each cluster on outcomes not used in the clustering, such as churn or revenue, and ask whether the groups behave differently and whether the team would treat them differently. If I can't describe a cluster in a sentence or act on it, it isn't a segment.

questions.key_insight: Segmentation succeeds or fails on feature choice and on whether the result is stable and easy to name, not on the algorithm.
questions.junior_answer: Standardize the features and run k-means.
questions.senior_answer: I'd start with the purpose: marketing, risk and service design each want different features. I'd engineer behavioral features (spend mix, balances, tenure, channel use), transform skewed ones, and scale. For mixed numeric and categorical data I'd use Gower distance with hierarchical clustering, k-prototypes, or reduce to embeddings or PCA components first. I'd compare candidate values of k on stability and interpretability, name segments from their profiles, and fit a shallow decision tree on the labels to explain the boundaries. I'd refresh on a schedule and track membership drift so campaigns don't target moving groups.

questions.key_insight: PCA rotates the data onto the directions of greatest variance, so it depends on feature scale and compresses linear structure only.
questions.junior_answer: It reduces dimensions by keeping the components with the most variance.
questions.senior_answer: PCA finds orthogonal directions that capture the most variance and projects the data onto the first few. That compresses correlated features, removes noise, and helps visualization or models hurt by collinearity. Because it chases variance, features must be standardized or large-scale features dominate. I'd choose components from cumulative explained variance or a scree plot, or by downstream model performance. Components are linear mixtures, so interpretation relies on loadings and gets hard. It is a poor fit when structure is non-linear, when tree models don't need it, or when you must explain individual features to stakeholders.

questions.key_insight: t-SNE and UMAP preserve local neighborhoods, not global distances or cluster sizes, so a picture of clusters is a hypothesis, not evidence.
questions.junior_answer: t-SNE is only for visualization, so I'd be careful.
questions.senior_answer: I'd say the plot is a good prompt but not proof. t-SNE (and UMAP to a lesser degree) preserves local neighborhoods while distorting global structure, so cluster sizes, the gaps between clusters and their relative positions aren't reliable. The picture also changes with perplexity, initialization and random seed, and can show apparent clusters in structureless noise. To test it I'd re-run with several settings and seeds, cluster in the original or PCA space and compare, check stability under resampling, and see whether the groups differ on outcomes the embedding never saw.

questions.junior_answer: Remove low-variance and correlated features, then use importance from a model.
questions.senior_answer: With many more features than the data supports, I'd start with cheap filters: drop constants, near-duplicates and highly correlated pairs, and apply domain judgment. Embedded methods such as lasso or tree-based importance then rank what remains, and wrapper methods such as recursive elimination can refine it at higher cost. The key discipline is doing selection inside each cross-validation fold; selecting on the whole dataset first leaks the labels into the validation score and inflates it. With regularized models or boosting, aggressive selection is often unnecessary, but it can help stability, speed and explainability.

questions.key_insight: Ensembling helps when the base models make different mistakes. When they are highly correlated or the system must stay simple, the gain doesn't justify the complexity.
questions.junior_answer: Combining models usually gives better accuracy, as in Kaggle.
questions.senior_answer: Averaging or stacking helps when models make different, partly uncorrelated errors, such as a boosted tree with a linear model or a neural net. Stacking trains a second-level model on the base models' out-of-fold predictions; using in-sample predictions would leak and overstate the benefit. Blending is the simpler version using a holdout set. Gains are typically small on clean tabular data where several boosted models are highly correlated. The costs are real: more training time, latency, monitoring and failure modes. I'd try a simple average first and ship the ensemble only if the gain beats the cost of maintaining it.

questions.question: Only 2% of your cases are positive. Compare resampling (including SMOTE), class weights and threshold tuning.

questions.key_insight: Imbalance is mostly a metric and threshold problem. Resampling changes what the model sees, so it must happen only inside training folds and often adds little over class weights.
questions.junior_answer: Use SMOTE to balance the classes.
questions.senior_answer: First I'd fix evaluation: accuracy is meaningless at 2%, so I'd use precision-recall, PR AUC and cost-based thresholds. Then compare options on honest folds. Class weights are the simplest: they change the loss without altering the data. Random undersampling is cheap but discards information; oversampling duplicates rows; SMOTE interpolates new minority points and can create unrealistic samples and overlap, and it must be applied only inside the training fold or synthetic points leak into validation. Resampling also distorts predicted probabilities, so I'd recalibrate. I'd try weights plus threshold tuning first and keep resampling only if it measurably helps.

questions.junior_answer: Use grid search with cross-validation.
questions.senior_answer: I'd first narrow the space to what matters for the model; for boosting that is learning rate, depth, number of rounds (with early stopping) and regularization. Random search usually beats a grid because only a few hyperparameters really matter and random draws try more distinct values of each; Bayesian optimization (for example Optuna) learns from earlier trials to choose promising ones and is worth it when each run is expensive. Repeated tuning on the same folds overfits them, so I'd keep a final holdout or use nested cross-validation to estimate the tuned procedure's performance, and stop when gains are within noise.

questions.key_insight: A network adjusts millions of weights a little at a time in the direction that reduces its error. Backpropagation is the efficient way to find that direction.
questions.junior_answer: It has layers of neurons and learns weights through backpropagation.
questions.senior_answer: A network is a stack of simple functions: each layer multiplies inputs by weights and applies a non-linear activation. Training starts with random weights, makes predictions, measures the error with a loss, then uses backpropagation, the chain rule applied layer by layer, to compute how much each weight contributed to the error. Gradient descent nudges every weight slightly to reduce it, and this repeats over many batches. Without the non-linearities the layers would collapse into one linear model. Typical problems are overfitting, unstable learning rates and vanishing gradients, handled with regularization, tuning and normalization.

questions.key_insight: All three step downhill on the loss. They differ in how much data each step uses and how they adapt the step size, and the learning rate is the most important setting of all.
questions.junior_answer: Adam is an adaptive version of gradient descent.
questions.senior_answer: Gradient descent moves the weights against the gradient of the loss computed on all the data; SGD uses one example or a mini-batch, which is far cheaper per step and adds noise that can help escape poor spots. Momentum smooths the steps. Adam keeps running averages of the gradient and its square and gives each weight its own effective step size, so it usually converges fast with little tuning. The learning rate matters most: too high and the loss oscillates or diverges, too low and it crawls or stalls. I'd use a warmup and decay schedule, watch loss curves, and note that well-tuned SGD with momentum sometimes generalizes slightly better.

questions.key_insight: The loss is the definition of wrong that the model optimizes, so it should match the cost of errors in the real decision.
questions.junior_answer: MSE for regression and cross-entropy for classification.
questions.senior_answer: The loss encodes what counts as an error. MSE penalizes large errors quadratically, so it targets the mean and is sensitive to outliers; MAE targets the median and is robust but has a constant gradient; Huber is quadratic for small errors and linear for large ones, a compromise. Cross-entropy (log loss) trains classifiers to output well-behaved probabilities and is smooth, unlike accuracy, which has no usable gradient. When errors have asymmetric business costs, such as under-forecasting being worse than over-forecasting, I'd use a quantile or custom weighted loss, and still evaluate with the metric the business uses.

questions.junior_answer: Add dropout and use early stopping.

Dropout randomly zeroes units during training so the network can't rely on any single path, which acts like averaging many sub-networks. Batch normalization standardizes layer inputs within each batch, which stabilizes gradients and allows higher learning rates; it has a mild regularizing side effect but is mainly an optimization aid. I'd first diagnose with train versus validation curves to be sure it is overfitting and not a leak or a bug.

questions.key_insight: A CNN reuses small filters across the whole image, so it detects a pattern wherever it appears with far fewer parameters than a fully connected network.
questions.junior_answer: CNNs use filters to detect features like edges.
questions.senior_answer: A convolutional layer slides a small filter over the input and records how strongly each location matches a pattern, such as an edge. Early layers detect simple patterns and deeper layers combine them into shapes and objects. Because the same filter is reused everywhere, the network needs far fewer parameters than a fully connected one and recognizes a pattern regardless of where it appears. Pooling summarizes regions and adds some tolerance to small shifts. The same idea works for any grid-like data with local structure, including audio spectrograms and some time series, although for most new work a pretrained model is the starting point.

questions.key_insight: Transformers process all tokens at once and let any token look directly at any other, which trains faster on modern hardware and handles long-range dependencies better.
questions.junior_answer: Transformers use attention and can be parallelized.
questions.senior_answer: RNNs and LSTMs read a sequence one step at a time, passing a hidden state forward. That is inherently sequential, so training can't be parallelized across positions, and information from early tokens has to survive many steps, which makes long-range dependencies hard. Transformers use attention so every token can directly weigh every other token, and all positions are processed in parallel, which maps well onto GPUs and scales with data and size. The cost is attention that grows quadratically with sequence length, which drives work on efficient variants and long-context methods. RNN-style models are still used for streaming or very small-footprint settings.

questions.key_insight: Attention lets each word decide how much to read from every other word, using a learned relevance score, and then blends their information accordingly.
questions.junior_answer: Attention lets the model focus on the important words.
questions.senior_answer: For each word, the model asks a question (the query) and compares it against a label (the key) on every other word; a high match means this word is relevant to me. Those match scores are turned into weights that sum to one, and the word's new representation is a weighted blend of the other words' content (their values). So in 'the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired', the representation of 'it' can pull in information from 'animal'. Scores are scaled so the softmax stays well behaved, and multiple heads let the model track different relationships, such as syntax and reference, at the same time.

questions.senior_answer: Training from scratch on 500 images would overfit, so I'd start from a model pretrained on a large dataset such as ImageNet, whose early layers already detect general patterns. First I'd freeze the backbone and train a new classification head, which is cheap and hard to overfit, then optionally unfreeze the top layers with a small learning rate. Augmentation (crops, flips, color jitter) and early stopping help, and I'd use stratified cross-validation since a single validation split of 100 images is noisy. If the domain is very different, such as medical scans, generic features may transfer less well, so I'd check against a baseline and consider a domain-specific pretrained model.

questions.senior_answer: I'd start with TF-IDF and logistic regression: it trains in seconds, needs little data, is easy to debug and often performs well when topics are signalled by distinctive words. TF-IDF weights words by how specific they are to a document but has no notion of meaning, so synonyms and paraphrases look unrelated. Embeddings from a pretrained model capture meaning and help on short or varied text, and they can feed the same simple classifier. An LLM can classify with few or no labels, at higher cost, latency and variability. I'd compare on one labeled test set for accuracy, cost per ticket and latency, and choose the simplest option that meets the target.

questions.key_insight: Words that appear in similar contexts get similar vectors, but a single vector per word cannot represent different meanings of the same word.
questions.junior_answer: They turn words into vectors so similar words are close together.
questions.senior_answer: word2vec trains a small network on a prediction task: given a word, predict its neighbors (skip-gram), or the reverse. The vectors that make that prediction work well end up placing words used in similar contexts near each other, following the idea that a word is defined by the company it keeps. Limits: each word has one vector regardless of sense, so 'bank' for rivers and 'bank' for money are blended; rare words get poor vectors; and embeddings absorb biases in the training text. Contextual embeddings from transformer models produce a different vector for each occurrence, which fixes much of the ambiguity problem.

questions.junior_answer: It's trained with human feedback to be more helpful.
questions.senior_answer: Stage one is pretraining on a huge text corpus to predict the next token, which gives broad knowledge but not good behavior. Stage two is supervised instruction tuning on examples of good responses so the model follows prompts. Stage three, RLHF, collects human comparisons between model answers, trains a reward model to predict which is preferred, and then optimizes the chat model against that reward with reinforcement learning while keeping it close to the original. The risk is that the reward model is only a proxy: models can learn to please raters, becoming sycophantic or verbose, which is why evaluation, diverse rater guidelines and newer preference-optimization methods matter.

questions.key_insight: Maximum likelihood picks the parameters that make the observed data most probable; many familiar loss functions are negative log-likelihoods in disguise.
questions.junior_answer: It finds the parameters that best fit the data by maximizing the probability of the data.
questions.senior_answer: Given a model with parameters, the likelihood is the probability it assigns to the data we saw. Maximum likelihood chooses the parameters that maximize it. For independent points the likelihood is a product, so we maximize the log, which turns it into a sum and avoids underflow. Squared error is the negative log-likelihood of Gaussian noise, and cross-entropy is the negative log-likelihood of Bernoulli labels, so training those models is maximum likelihood. It can fail with little data, where it overfits, and with perfectly separable classes, where logistic coefficients diverge; priors or regularization fix both.

questions.junior_answer: I would run a chi-square test on the conversion counts and then compare channels in pairs.
questions.senior_answer: Conversions are counts in a channel-by-outcome table, so a chi-square test of independence asks whether conversion rate depends on channel. It needs independent users and reasonably large expected counts; otherwise use Fisher's exact test. A significant result only says some channels differ. To find which, I'd run pairwise comparisons with a correction such as Holm or Tukey rather than six uncorrected tests, and report effect sizes with intervals, since a huge sample makes tiny differences significant. For revenue per user the analogue is ANOVA, or a rank-based test if the data are heavily skewed.

questions.junior_answer: A bandit sends more traffic to the better option while it learns, so you lose less.
questions.senior_answer: A bandit shifts traffic toward better-performing variants as evidence accumulates, which cuts the cost of showing a loser. That fits headline testing, promotions and recommendations, where options are many, decisions are short-lived and the goal is reward, not a report. An A/B test fits product changes where you need an unbiased estimate, a guardrail check and a decision you can defend. With a bandit the unequal, adaptive allocation makes estimates for the weaker arms noisy and biased and complicates p-values. Thompson sampling draws a plausible rate for each arm from its posterior and plays the best draw. If the effect drifts, for example by day of week, a bandit can lock onto a stale winner unless it discounts old data.

Averaging observed lifetimes of churned customers biases the answer downward, and treating active customers as churned at today's date is also wrong. Survival analysis handles this censoring. A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates the share still subscribed at each tenure, and I would compare curves by plan or cohort. To include features I'd use a Cox proportional hazards model, which gives hazard ratios, after checking that the proportionality assumption holds. If the goal is a score for who will churn in the next 30 days, a classifier on a fixed window can be simpler.

questions.junior_answer: ARIMA uses past values of the series to predict future values.
questions.senior_answer: ARIMA combines autoregression on past values (p), differencing to remove trend (d) and a moving average of past errors (q). Differencing aims at a stationary series, whose mean and variance don't drift, because the model's coefficients assume stable relationships. I'd choose orders using autocorrelation plots and information criteria, then check them by walk-forward validation. It works well for a single, short, regular series with few external drivers and is easy to explain. It is a poor fit for many series at once, multiple seasonalities, holidays and rich external features, where boosted trees or other models do better.

questions.question: Which models need feature scaling, and which don't? Why?

follow_ups.text: What goes wrong if you fit the scaler on all the data?

questions.key_insight: Scaling matters when a model uses distances or penalizes coefficient size, or when optimization is sensitive to scale; tree models split on order and don't care.
questions.junior_answer: Neural networks and SVMs need scaling, trees don't.
questions.senior_answer: Models based on distances (k-NN, k-means, SVMs), penalized models (ridge, lasso) and gradient-based models like neural networks are sensitive to feature scale: a feature measured in large units dominates distances or gets penalized differently. Tree-based models split on thresholds, so monotonic rescaling changes nothing. I fit the scaler on the training data only and apply it to validation and test data, otherwise information leaks. Standardization is the default; min-max suits bounded inputs but is sensitive to outliers, where a robust scaler helps.

questions.key_insight: The algorithm is short; the care goes into initialization, empty clusters and stopping, plus running it several times because the result depends on the start.
questions.junior_answer: I would pick random centers, assign points and update the means in a loop.
questions.senior_answer: Initialize k centers by sampling points (ideally k-means++), then repeat: compute distances from every point to every center with broadcasting, assign each point to its nearest center with argmin, and set each center to the mean of its points. If a cluster is empty, re-seed it from a far-away point. Stop when assignments stop changing or the centers move less than a tolerance, with an iteration cap. Run it several times with different seeds and keep the lowest within-cluster sum of squares. Before trusting it I'd check that features are scaled and that the clusters are stable and interpretable.

follow_ups.text: Why does unscaled data make this slow or unstable?

questions.key_insight: Compute the gradient of the mean squared error, step against it, and watch the loss curve: a good learning rate decreases it smoothly and a bad one diverges or crawls.
questions.junior_answer: I would repeatedly update the weights by subtracting the learning rate times the gradient.
questions.senior_answer: With X as an n by d matrix, predictions are X @ w, the gradient of mean squared error is (2/n) * X.T @ (X @ w - y), and each step is w -= lr * gradient, repeated for a fixed number of iterations or until the loss stops improving. I'd scale features first, because very different scales make the loss surface a narrow valley that forces a tiny learning rate. I'd plot loss per iteration: smooth decline means the rate is fine, oscillation or growth means it is too high, and a very slow decline means it is too low. The closed form is exact for small problems; gradient descent scales to large ones and generalizes to other models. Mini-batches trade noisier steps for much cheaper updates.

follow_ups.text: Why cosine similarity instead of Euclidean distance?

follow_ups.text: How does it handle synonyms?

follow_ups.text: How would it scale to millions of documents?

How would you avoid comparing a query against every one of millions of documents?

questions.key_insight: TF-IDF search matches words, not meaning: fast and transparent, but blind to synonyms and paraphrase.
questions.junior_answer: I would convert documents to TF-IDF vectors and rank them by cosine similarity to the query.
questions.senior_answer: Fit a TF-IDF vectorizer on the documents to get a sparse matrix, transform the query with the same vectorizer, compute cosine similarity as a sparse dot product (rows are L2-normalized by default), and return the top-scoring documents with argsort. Cosine ignores document length, which Euclidean distance does not. The limits are that it only matches shared words, so synonyms and paraphrases are missed, and that stop words and tokenization choices matter. At large scale I'd use an inverted index such as BM25 in a search engine, or embeddings with an approximate nearest-neighbor index, often combining both.

questions.key_insight: LoRA freezes the base model and trains small added matrices, giving most of the benefit of fine-tuning at a fraction of the memory and storage.
questions.junior_answer: LoRA is cheaper than full fine-tuning because it trains fewer parameters.
questions.senior_answer: LoRA keeps the pretrained weights frozen and learns small low-rank matrices added to selected layers, so only a tiny share of parameters is trained. That cuts GPU memory, speeds up training and lets you store one small adapter per task and swap them on one base model. Full fine-tuning can capture larger changes in behavior but costs far more and risks forgetting. I'd use LoRA for style, format or domain adaptation with limited data and budget. Before either, I'd check whether prompting or retrieval solves the problem, since fine-tuning is better for behavior than for adding facts.
